key_insight: Reported gains from randomly perturbing language-model weights may not require discovering hidden task-specific experts. Keeping the model frozen and adding random biases to its output logits can match or exceed full-weight perturbations in the reported comparisons.
problem_solved: Tests whether improvements attributed to dense neighborhoods of experts in weight space actually require that geometric explanation—or can arise from simpler changes to model outputs.
method: Reproduce the gains reported for random Gaussian perturbations of pretrained language-model weights.
Restrict perturbations to a single decoder block and assess how much of the improvement remains.
Compare weight perturbations with random output-logit biases while keeping all model weights frozen.
impact: Practitioners should test simple output-level baselines before attributing performance gains to hidden experts in weight space. The findings suggest that useful gains may be possible without modifying model weights.
visual_elements: Three-path diagram contrasting full-weight perturbation, single-block perturbation, and frozen-model logit bias.
Qualitative comparison chart highlighting substantial gains from one-block perturbation and competitive performance from logit bias, without inventing numerical values.
Frozen-model icon feeding into an adjustable output-logit layer.
Hypothesis-versus-evidence panel contrasting nearby weight-space experts with a simpler output-level alternative.
paper_title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
paper_authors: Nicolas Dufour, Elouan Gardès, Amil Dravid, Patrick Pérez, Loic Landrieu
